newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Majors dominate latest U.S. Gulf lease sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Majors dominate latest U.S. Gulf lease sale.

text.p: The major oil companies dominated the latest Gulf of Mexico lease round on Wednesday, but independents made a splash of their own with a push into deepwater plays off the Texas and Louisiana coast.

Shell Offshore Inc was high bidder on the day, winning rights to explore for oil and natural gas on 123 tracts in the federal waters off the coast of Texas and western Louisiana after submitting $62.1 million in high bids, the U.S. Minerals Management Service said.

A bidding war of sorts erupted in the Alaminos Canyon area, where several bids were placed on blocks south of Shell's Baha play in 7,620 feet of water, site of the deepest well ever spudded in the Gulf of Mexico.

"When you see multiple interest like that, everybody's got a seismic (survey) that shows a bright spot," an indication of possible hydrocarbons, said Blake Wright, an analyst tracking Gulf drilling for Offshore Data Services.

In addition to the Shell Oil Co unit, exploration and production units of Chevron Corp, Texaco Inc, Conoco Inc, Mobil Corp, Phillips Petroleum Co and Amoco Corp were among the top ten bidders in the lease sale.

The lease round was the largest ever in terms of the number of bids received and third largest in terms of revenues produced on the sale of rights to explore in federal waters in the western section of the Gulf. Producers bid on a total of 929 blocks, submitting winning bids totalling $352.5 million.
"That's a pretty strong western sale," said Chris Oynes, regional director of the federal agency.

The record bidding was fueled in large part by lower royalty rates in effect for the first time on production from deepwater sections of the western Gulf, part of the federal government's push to boost domestic production.

Western Gulf tracts in water deeper than 800 metres drew 321 bids in the lease sale, up from 74 bids in the western lease round last year and nine bids in the 1994 sale, according to the Minerals Management Service, an agency of the U.S. Department of Interior.

Improvements in three-dimensional seismic surveys, used to identify potential oil and natural gas fields, also sparked interest in shallower Gulf plays. Producers bid on 184 western Gulf blocks in less than 200 metres of water this year, up from 129 last year.

Anadarko Petroleum Corp and Louisiana Land and Exploration were among the active independents in the deep water, an area still dominated by the majors. The two independents teamed up to place winning bids on several blocks in Alaminos Canyon, a section of the Gulf east of Corpus Christi, Texas where water depths approach 8,000 feet.
Vastar Resources, an active player in the shallower sections of the Gulf, also pushed into deeper waters in the western Gulf after making a similar move in the central Gulf sale earlier this year.

But the majors dominated bidding in the deepwater, extending their control of tracts in Alaminos Canyon and Keathley Canyon. Shell, which spudded its Baha well last April, bid between $1.2 million and $3.5 million to win lease rights on three blocks even deeper in the canyon.

Shell also teamed up with Amoco and Texaco in a consortium to bid on several blocks in the canyon, and ended up bidding against the consortium to win drilling rights outright on three of those blocks.
